title: Letters of direction (Francis de Sales)
hook: his letters advise patience with oneself above all
tomorrow: what if you were made for a job no one will ever spell out?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius told his life as the pilgrim: not a hero who'd arrived, a student still on the road. The line was the pilgrim.

Two captains in a locker room after a loss. One says: be furious with yourselves, that's how you get better. The other says: own it, learn it, go again. Both want the same thing, to win next time. People of faith argue a version of this about their own faults. And a bishop named Francis de Sales spent years writing to people who kept failing at the same things, one letter at a time. He picked a side, and he had reasons.
screen: `TWO CAPTAINS AFTER A LOSS.` → `FURY, OR GO AGAIN?` → `A BISHOP WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the form. A book speaks to anyone who opens it. A letter of direction speaks to one person: her household, her temper, her dry prayers this month. Francis de Sales wrote letters like this to friends such as Jane de Chantal, and to people living ordinary lives in the world. Second, the case for being hard on yourself, and it's a real one. Faults matter. Catholics examine their consciences and confess their sins because wrongdoing hurts God's friendship and other people. Anger at your own failure can look like caring, and going easy can look like not caring at all. Third, Francis's answer, the advice his letters keep coming back to: patience with yourself. He agrees faults matter. But in his book on the devout life he says that getting angry with yourself over a fault doesn't heal it; it piles a second trouble on the first. A father's gentle correction, he writes, does more than a furious one. So you notice, you're sorry, and you begin again, without being shocked that you needed to. Fourth, why a letter suits that advice. A sermon is heard once. A letter gets folded, kept in a drawer, and read again on the bad day. Slow advice, sent slowly, to someone changing slowly.
screen: `ONE LETTER, ONE LIFE.` · `THE CASE FOR BEING HARD ON YOURSELF.` · `PATIENCE: NOTICE, BE SORRY, BEGIN AGAIN.` · `A LETTER WAITS IN A DRAWER.` · then, large: `HAVE PATIENCE WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: With a pen and a scrap of paper, write two lines to someone who is being hard on themselves right now: no advice, just patience, the way Francis wrote. If you pray, hold them by name while the ink dries.
Letters of direction. Personal letters of spiritual guidance, written to one person about their own life. Today's word.
Hold onto this: have patience with yourself, because faults matter and so does beginning again. Talk soon.

howItsDone: Some Catholics have a spiritual director they meet or write to for guidance, and collections of Francis de Sales's letters are still read for that kind of counsel.

fork.setup: your teammate says being hard on yourself is how you get better. Francis says patience. what is her side's strongest point?
options: she takes her faults seriously and wants real change.
she secretly enjoys feeling bad about herself.
she thinks faults don't matter unless people see them.
fork.reveal: that's the best case for her side, and Francis agrees faults matter. his letters ask for change that's patient: be sorry, and begin again without shock.
